lessons.title: Monetary Transmission: From Repo Rate to the Real Economy

body.text: A repo rate cut does not automatically become cheaper EMIs and stronger GDP growth. It has to travel through five different channels, each with its own leaks, lags and blockages, before it shows up anywhere in the real economy.

children.text: The Five Channels of Monetary Transmission

Lesson 2 in Chapter 1 covered how a rate change reaches your own loan through EBLR versus MCLR. That is one piece of a larger picture. Textbook monetary economics identifies five distinct channels through which a policy rate change eventually reaches output and inflation, and a professional macro read tracks all five, because they do not always move together, and they do not always move at the same speed.

body.caption: The five channels of monetary transmission

cells: Policy rate moves money market rates, which move bank lending and deposit rates
A repo cut lowers EBLR-linked home loan EMIs within a quarter
Banks' balance sheet health and risk appetite amplify or dampen how much of a rate change gets passed on as actual credit growth
Banks with high NPAs historically passed on cuts more slowly, worried about margin pressure
Lower rates raise the present value of future cash flows, lifting equity valuations and property prices, creating a wealth effect
Falling bond yields typically support Nifty P/E multiples, and cheaper home loans support real estate demand
Lower domestic rates narrow the interest differential with economies like the US, which can pressure the rupee
A widening India-US rate gap has historically coincided with periods of rupee weakness and FPI debt outflows
Forward guidance shapes how households and businesses expect future rates and inflation to behave, influencing spending and investment decisions today
A credible accommodative stance can pull forward capex decisions even before a single rate cut is delivered

cards.definition: Policy rate moves lending and deposit rates directly
Bank balance sheet health determines how much of a rate move becomes actual credit
Lower rates lift equity and property valuations, creating a wealth effect
Rate differentials with other economies move the rupee
Forward guidance shapes spending and investment decisions before rates actually move

children.text: The Interest Rate Corridor: Repo Is the Middle, Not the Whole Picture

markDefs.definition: Standing Deposit Facility: the rate at which banks can park surplus funds with the RBI overnight, without any collateral. It forms the floor of the RBI's interest rate corridor.
Marginal Standing Facility: the rate at which banks can borrow overnight funds from the RBI against government securities, usually at a premium to the repo rate. It forms the ceiling of the corridor.

Weighted Average Call Rate: the average interest rate on unsecured overnight borrowing between banks in the call money market. The RBI's actual operating target, which it tries to keep close to the repo rate through daily liquidity operations.

children.text: The repo rate is a policy signal, not the actual rate at which money changes hands overnight in the banking system. The RBI runs a corridor: the
, sits below the repo rate as a floor, and the
sits above it as a ceiling. Day to day, the RBI's real operating target is the
Weighted Average Call Rate, or WACR
, the rate at which banks actually lend to each other overnight, which it tries to keep close to the repo rate using daily liquidity operations.

body.label: Typical corridor width
body.context: Illustrative: with repo at 5.50%, SDF would sit near 5.25% and MSF near 5.75%. The exact corridor width has been recalibrated by the RBI before, so confirm the current width rather than assuming it is fixed.

body.title: For the technically curious: how the RBI actually targets WACR

markDefs.definition: Variable Rate Repo and Variable Rate Reverse Repo: auction-based tools the RBI uses to inject or absorb liquidity from the banking system at a market-discovered rate, rather than a fixed administered rate, used for fine daily and weekly liquidity management between MPC meetings.

children.text: If systemic liquidity is in surplus, banks have more cash than they need and overnight rates drift toward the SDF floor. If liquidity is in deficit, banks scramble for funds and rates drift toward the MSF ceiling. To keep WACR anchored close to the repo rate in between, the RBI runs
Variable Rate Repo and Variable Rate Reverse Repo

auctions, injecting funds when liquidity is tight and absorbing funds when it is loose, on top of the CRR and OMO tools covered earlier. None of this changes the policy rate itself. It is plumbing work that decides whether the policy rate actually holds in the market, or drifts away from it.
Why Transmission in India Is Often Incomplete

Three frictions routinely blunt how much of a rate cut actually reaches the real economy in India. First, banks are slow to cut deposit rates as fast as lending rates, because they fear losing depositors to small savings schemes, whose rates are administered by the government and do not move in lockstep with the repo rate. Second, systemic liquidity conditions matter: transmission works faster and more fully when the banking system is liquidity-surplus, and slower and more partially when it is liquidity-deficit, regardless of what the repo rate itself says. Third, NBFCs, which fund a large share of retail and small business credit, borrow mainly from wholesale markets rather than deposits, so their funding costs track corporate bond spreads as much as the repo rate, meaning a repo cut does not automatically cheapen an NBFC's own cost of funds by the same amount.

body.title: A Cut That Does Not Show Up
body.scenario: The MPC cuts the repo rate by 25 basis points. Two weeks later, systemic liquidity has slipped into deficit because of quarterly advance tax outflows pulling cash out of the banking system, and the WACR is trading noticeably above the new, lower repo rate.
body.prompt: What is happening to transmission in this window, and what tool would you expect the RBI to use to fix it?
body.modelAnswer: Even though the policy rate has been cut, the actual overnight rate banks are transacting at (WACR) is trading above it because the banking system does not have enough surplus cash, a liquidity deficit is pushing money market rates toward the MSF ceiling rather than letting them settle near the new repo rate. The RBI would typically inject liquidity through Variable Rate Repo auctions, or through OMO bond purchases, to bring systemic liquidity back into surplus and pull WACR back down closer to the repo rate, effectively letting the actual rate cut show up in the money market, not just on paper.

children.text: From Repo Rate to Real Economy: Consumption, Investment, Housing

Once transmission actually works, its effects show up in three broad places. Lower EMIs on EBLR-linked loans free up disposable income, supporting discretionary consumption, auto sales and consumer durables. Lower corporate borrowing costs improve the arithmetic on capex projects that were marginal at higher rates, supporting private investment, though this channel is typically the slowest to show up, since capex decisions take quarters to plan and execute even after financing gets cheaper. And lower mortgage rates directly improve housing affordability, which is why real estate and housing finance stocks are among the most rate-sensitive sectors on NSE and BSE.

body.title: Which Channel Is This?
body.question: The RBI cuts the repo rate and signals more cuts are likely ahead. Even before any loan gets repriced, the Nifty rallies and stays elevated for weeks on expectations of a sustained easing cycle. Which transmission channel best explains this immediate market move?
options: The interest rate channel, since lending rates have already fallen
The credit channel, since banks have already expanded lending
The asset price and expectations channels working together, since equity valuations react to the expected future rate path, not just the single decision already made
The exchange rate channel, since a weaker rupee is boosting exporter earnings
body.explanation: Equity markets are forward-looking. A rally that happens before any loan actually reprices is being driven by the asset price channel (lower expected future rates raise the present value of future earnings, supporting P/E multiples) combined with the expectations channel (the market is pricing in an entire anticipated easing cycle, not just the single cut delivered). The interest rate and credit channels take quarters to show up in actual lending data, far slower than an equity market reaction.

body.title: Corridor Math
body.prompt: The repo rate is 5.50% and the RBI's interest rate corridor is symmetric at 25 basis points on either side. What is the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate?
body.explanation: The MSF sits 25 basis points above the repo rate as the ceiling of the corridor: 5.50% plus 0.25% equals 5.75%. The SDF, by the same logic, would sit at 5.25% as the floor.

body.title: Checking Whether Transmission Is Actually Working
steps: Compare WACR to the repo rate; a persistent gap signals a liquidity problem, not a policy problem
Check whether systemic liquidity is in surplus or deficit, since this determines how fast and how fully rate changes pass through
Track how quickly banks move deposit rates, not just lending rates, since deposit repricing lags are a common transmission bottleneck
Watch NBFC bond spreads separately from the repo rate, since NBFC funding costs do not move one-for-one with the policy rate
Give the credit and investment channels several quarters before judging whether a rate move has worked; the asset price and expectations channels move first, the real economy follows

body.text: Nothing in this lesson is investment advice. It is educational content on how monetary policy transmits through the financial system to the real economy, consistent with SEBI's guidelines for registered research analysts on this platform.

points: Monetary policy reaches the real economy through five channels: interest rate, credit, asset price, exchange rate and expectations, and they do not all move at the same speed
The repo rate is a policy signal; the RBI's actual operating target is WACR, kept near the repo rate through a corridor bounded by the SDF floor and MSF ceiling
Deposit rate stickiness, systemic liquidity conditions, and NBFC dependence on wholesale funding are the three biggest reasons transmission in India is often incomplete or delayed
Asset prices and market expectations typically react before a single loan reprices; consumption follows over months, and investment and capex typically follow over quarters
A rate cut that is not showing up in WACR is usually a liquidity management problem the RBI can address with VRR auctions or OMOs, not evidence the rate cut failed
